The FBI calls it a "sophisticated, multi-layer scam" that targets seniors.

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

A similar incident happened in Wisconsin, where an individual said she was using Facebook on a laptop when a pop-up message claimed there was a virus, according to the Marquette County Sheriff's Office. The message showed a phone number that could be called to secure personal information.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

When the victim called the number, a man answered and said the call was being transferred to the Federal Trade Commission's fraud department. Scammers then allegedly told the victim someone had tried to drain their savings account through a wire transfer, but it was blocked.

SEND US A TIP

To protect their assets, the victim was allegedly told to withdraw their savings, convert the money into gold bars and wait for an "officer" to collect them at home. Following those instructions, the victim bought gold bars, photographed them and bagged them for pickup.

The sheriff's office said the victim spent much of Oct. 20 on the phone with a man who called himself "Sam." When a sheriff's deputy arrived at the home and the victim mentioned it, "Sam" ordered them to hang up, tell the deputy nothing and call back once he was gone.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

When the victim resumed speaking with "Sam," they were instructed to take the bag with gold outside and wait for the courier to arrive. Law enforcement caught the man who picked up the gold, who was identified as Dhavalkumar Dashrathgiri Bava. He was taken into custody on charges of felony conspiracy to commit theft of more than $100,000 by false representation, with an enhanced penalty because the victim was elderly.

TRUMP ADMIN’S FRAUD CRACKDOWN TARGETS FOREIGNERS ACCUSED OF INFILTRATING US FEDERAL PROGRAMS

Tom Hyslip, former Secret Service agent and professor of cybercrime at the University of South Florida, told Fox News Digital that the scam is operated by "organized criminal gangs."

"A lot of them operate out of Africa. There's been many indictments of arrests over the years for these types of scams. And they've been going around for years and the criminals keep changing their MO. It used to be the Nigerian Prince. And then it went to the investment scheme or someone's been kidnapped," Hyslip said.

"So now they're trying to take their time, pretend they're from a government agency or your bank, build that rapport, build the trust, then they make the ask."

item.title: The next generation of workers is taking its talent and spending power to this Southern state
item.description: South Carolina posted the largest net gain of Gen Z adults through interstate migration in 2024, but California lost more than 58,000 young residents.
item.content:encoded:
The next generation of workers is on the move, and South Carolina is drawing more young adults than any other state.

The Palmetto State recorded a net gain of 22,843 Gen Z adults through interstate migration in 2024, according to a new LendingTree analysis. The study defines Gen Z as adults ages 18 to 27, the generation that follows millennials.

LendingTree chief consumer finance analyst Matt Schulz told Fox News Digital that affordability and job prospects may help explain the state’s appeal. South Carolina’s proximity to Charlotte, he said, gives young adults access to a growing job market while potentially offering a less expensive place to live.

"Gen Z is at the most mobile time of their lives, and they’re looking for a place where they can live affordably, where there are decent jobs and good opportunity," Schulz said.

RED STATES HAVE SPENT DECADES DOMINATING A KEY CORNER OF THE ECONOMY

California had the largest net loss of Gen Z residents, at 58,109. Texas was the most popular destination for those leaving, drawing 19,287 Californians.

Schulz said California, New Jersey and New York had some of the largest net losses, while South Carolina, Missouri, Tennessee and Texas posted net gains. But he said young adults are also looking for career opportunities and a lifestyle they can afford.

"Ultimately, it is about looking for job opportunity and looking for the best place to get started with your career and being able to afford the things that you want to do and have the life you want to live," he said.

AMERICANS KEEP MOVING TO TEXAS AND FLORIDA — BUT ONE OTHER RED STATE IS GROWING EVEN FASTER

The figures build on a broader migration trend.

South Carolina added more than 59,000 residents from other states between 2022 and 2023, gaining roughly $4.1 billion in income, according to IRS data cited in an earlier Fox News Digital analysis.

The state had the nation’s largest per-capita net gain, while Texas and Florida drew more newcomers overall.

Schulz said young adults’ moves can have broader economic implications as they enter the workforce, start families and make major purchases.

"These are the future leaders of your country and the future business owners and parents," he said. "The future of our economy depends a lot on what Gen Z does, whether it’s the housing market or auto loans or starting small businesses."

item.title: JOHN MIZE: Democrat victory just means the fight for life has added importance
item.description: Tuesday, Nov. 3 election losses leave mifepristone's pending review among several vital pro-life battlegrounds, as we face a pro-abortion Congress.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday, Nov. 3, Americans cast their votes and turned congressional majorities against the pro-life cause.

It may be easy to despair, especially following two years of strong, pro-life leadership that accomplished a historic year of defunding many abortion providers from federal Medicaid dollars, but the pro-life movement has fought through hostile waters before — and won.

Here’s how we navigate the next two years.

STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE

Defending legacy pro-life provisions must be a first priority. We have known for months that the Hyde Amendment, protecting taxpayers from being forced to directly fund abortions, has been in the crosshairs for the next pro-abortion Congress.

But conscience protections for healthcare entities that choose not to provide abortions under the Weldon Amendment may also be on the line.

This pro-abortion majority wants to make Americans complicit in their extremism.

Both the Hyde and Weldon amendments have survived pro-abortion majorities before, including the 117th Congress. In 2021, the House Appropriations Committee advanced a Labor, Health and Human Services, and Education spending bill that omitted both Hyde and Weldon rider language.

Even though both chambers were led by pro-abortion majorities, pro-life organizations were able to rally, telling Congress that these protections are not up for negotiation.

This is the same message we must carry over the next two years.

Congress must also be reminded that preserving these riders is in its own best interest, attaining bipartisan public support.

According to the 2026 Knights of Columbus/Marist polling, 54% of Americans opposed taxpayer funding of abortion and 63% support conscience protections for healthcare providers.

'EXTREMIST' AND 'BARBARIC': MASSACHUSETTS DEMOCRATS BREAK RANKS OVER NEW ABORTION LAW

Pro-abortion members of Congress are also likely to urge the passage of the Women’s Health Protection Act. This bill is intended to codify the state of abortion extremism under Roe v. Wade, preventing any state or locality from restricting abortion before viability.

If this became law, it would also erase necessary safeguards for women like mandatory ultrasounds to confirm pregnancy or rule out ectopic pregnancies, eliminate waiting periods and allow unrestricted mail-order abortion.

What pro-life groups have more accurately called the "Women’s Health Endangerment Act" has been fended off since it was first introduced in 2013. Under the 117th Congress, this bill passed the House of Representatives but did not reach the 60-vote threshold needed to overcome cloture in the Senate.

However, this new Congress is signaling less political restraint and may eliminate the filibuster to evade the necessary checks and balances of cloture. Pro-life groups must be unified in opposing this extreme tactic.

It is essential to remember that Congress is only one cog in the political machine, and we can still fight for life within the Trump administration and among the many states.

The pro-life movement has overcome many cycles of pro-abortion control since Roe and yet still was able to achieve the historic victory in Dobbs not too long after the 117th Congress.

FIRST ON FOX: TOP REPUBLICANS TAKE ABORTION PILL FIGHT TO SUPREME COURT, CITING COERCION AND SAFETY RISKS

Administrative agency action is still on the table. The Food and Drug Administration’s review of the abortion pill is still pending, and its latest update to the courts suggests final results will be available to the public by March 2027.

Restoring in-person dispensing requirements as a minimum repair to mifepristone’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy is still on the table. It’s even more essential now that the agency’s review is airtight and able to withstand partisan scrutiny.

The Trump administration still has the authority to finally rescind the Biden-era Office of Legal Counsel’s politicized Comstock opinion and fully enforce the law through the Department of Justice.

Stopping the mail-order abortion scheme harming women across the country will be essential to combatting the losses of this week.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Still, we must not waver from our collective efforts in all 50 states. Losses in Texas showed us that we cannot become complacent in protecting life where we believe it to be the most secure.

American politics is a cultural battle and, as Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia stated, "[t]he permissibility of abortion, and the limitations upon it, are to be resolved like most important questions in our democracy: by citizens trying to persuade one another and then voting."

item.title: PAUL TELLER: Foreign investors are milking US taxpayers. Congress should stop them
item.description: Foreign investors are financing American lawsuits and paying zero tax on their winnings, a loophole Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calls "a malignancy."
item.content:encoded:
America has become too litigious. Even the slightest wrong seems to yield a lawsuit these days, lining the pockets of trial attorneys who profit from pitting Americans against Americans. But did you know that a new brand of lawsuit has emerged in recent years that has foreigners fueling the litigation and then taking the winnings at a lower — or even zero — tax rate?

That’s not fair and needs to stop.

Here’s how it works. A foreign sovereign wealth fund or other investment fund overseas eyes a potential or existing lawsuit in the United States and speculates that it could earn a significant financial return by contracting with one party, often the plaintiff’s side, to underwrite the large and growing costs of the lawsuit. When the plaintiff receives a financial reward from the court, the winnings tend to be taxed as ordinary income (i.e., at a higher rate).

WAVE OF OVERLOOKED 'LEFT-WING' LAWSUITS COULD COME WITH AN UNEXPECTED PRICE TAG FOR AMERICANS

But when the foreign underwriter that financed that same lawsuit collects its share of the winnings (decided in advance as a condition of funding the lawsuit), that money can be treated as a capital gain and therefore taxed at a lower rate than the plaintiff herself pays. And since foreign investors generally owe no U.S. tax on capital gains from American sources, the tax rate for the foreigner is often zero, even as the American plaintiff pays the ordinary income tax rate.

Again — not fair and needs to stop.

TREASURY FLAGS $8B IN SUSPICIOUS FOREIGN-DIRECTED TRANSFERS THROUGH US MONEY SERVICES FIRMS

Recently, in a Capitol Hill hearing, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent sharply criticized this scheme of foreigners fueling American lawsuits and running away with a greater share of the winnings. Bessent is exactly right: Foreign financing of American lawsuits is indeed "a malignancy" on our judicial system, as he called it, that is draining money out of the U.S. economy, driving up prices across the board for American consumers and further encouraging litigiousness in American society.

As the secretary noted, these foreign financiers are asserting preferential tax treatment, avoiding U.S. taxes entirely and getting away with it. The result: American taxpayers are in fact subsidizing a practice that is driving up costs for American businesses and fostering higher prices for all Americans at the grocery store and at the pump.

SUPREME COURT CLIMATE CASE COULD BANKRUPT OIL COMPANIES, SEND GAS PRICES SOARING, EXPERTS WARN

Unbelievable!

What’s particularly offensive about this practice is that the impetus behind the capital gains tax rate being lower than the ordinary income tax rate on the same amount of money is the wholeheartedly American desire to reward risk-taking investment aimed at production and growth. But the foreign hedge funds and other international wealth funds that underwrite American lawsuits at the lower or zero tax rate are not investing in economic growth. Quite the opposite. They are seeking to profit from the restraint of growth, from lawsuits that siphon resources from the profit margins and bottom lines of American producers.

REPUBLICANS AREN’T STOPPING: GOP TO UNLEASH ANOTHER ‘BIG, BEAUTIFUL BILL’ WITH A NEW TARGET

Outrageous!

Congress should close this un-American, abusive loophole this year and put the billions of dollars in increased revenue toward pro-growth tax relief in America. In typical Beltway fashion, some politicos will assert that there’s not enough time to make this fix this year. That’s inaccurate. Right now, Congress is scheduled to be in session for at least five more weeks this calendar year, and there is room in the calendar to schedule additional days and (God forbid!) late nights in session. Yes, this might mean coming back to the office after scurrying around town to lavish holiday parties, but so be it. This issue is worth it.

DOJ UNVEILS NATIONWIDE TAX FRAUD CRACKDOWN INVOLVING 76 DEFENDANTS, NEARLY $500M IN ALLEGED LOSSES

Many in Congress, including House Republican leaders, have said that this year they want to pass another "reconciliation" bill (a special type of legislation not subject to the Senate filibuster, regarding revenues going in and out of the Treasury). That would be the ideal legislative vehicle in which to fix this foreign loophole and direct the resulting revenues back to the American taxpayer.

But if Congress can't get its act together soon, the White House should work with Bessent to see what actions the executive branch may legally take on its own to address this boon for foreign financiers.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Either way, this would be an easy win for American consumers and businesses, while defunding left-wing trial attorneys who continue to enrich themselves on the backs of excessive lawsuits.

Let's get this done.

item.title: EXCLUSIVE: Trump's FAA touts new AI-powered tool helping thousands of passengers avoid flight delays
item.description: The Trump administration's SMART system rerouted nearly 180 flights carrying 24,000 passengers, cutting flight times by over 10 minutes on average.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: The Trump administration's new AI-supported air traffic management tool has already helped reroute nearly 180 flights carrying approximately 24,000 passengers to avoid congestion, cutting flight times by more than 10 minutes on average, according to new Department of Transportation (DOT) data shared exclusively with Fox News Digital.

The Federal Aviation Administration's (FAA) Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories system, known as SMART, has been operational for nearly six weeks, helping air traffic controllers identify more fuel-efficient routes and anticipate potential disruptions.

According to DOT, the technology has also saved nearly 80 gallons of fuel per flight on average, offering an early glimpse of how the Trump administration hopes to reduce flight delays and cancellations.

TRUMP UNVEILS AMERICA.GOV AS AI-POWERED HUB FOR PASSPORTS, MEDICARE ENROLLMENT AND MORE

"Under President Trump, we are making historic progress to revitalize air traffic control and improve the passenger experience for millions of Americans," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement provided to Fox News Digital.

Duffy also said the technology would deliver broader benefits as the program expands.

"SMART will slash frustrating delays, reduce stress on air traffic controllers, and lower travel prices."

One example came in October when a flight carrying 147 passengers from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to Orlando International Airport avoided expected congestion after SMART recommended an alternative route.

SEVERE TURBULENCE DIVERTS NEW YORK CITY FLIGHT TO MIAMI, 8 INJURED

The flight had been scheduled to depart during a period when congestion was expected along its original path. SMART identified a route farther west, which air traffic controllers accepted, shortening the journey by 11 nautical miles and saving six minutes of flight time, according to DOT.

The technology combines 200 data streams, including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics, into a centralized platform.

Its AI-supported engine helps aviation specialists anticipate where congestion could develop and recommend more efficient routes before congestion builds.

The technology is also designed to improve how the FAA manages severe weather, a source of disruptions for U.S. air travelers.

PILOTLESS CARGO AIRCRAFT COULD CHANGE HOW PACKAGES MOVE

According to a DOT fact sheet, the agency's existing approach involves blocking off large rectangular sections of airspace affected by storms, even though weather systems are often irregularly shaped, and safe corridors may remain available.

SMART is intended to provide a clearer picture of changing weather conditions, allowing aviation specialists to identify routes around storms and determine when restricted airspace can safely reopen.

Despite its AI-supported capabilities, SMART does not independently direct aircraft or replace human air traffic controllers.

A team of aviation specialists analyzes and validates SMART's data before sending scheduling recommendations to the FAA's Air Traffic Control System Command Center. Those recommendations are then forwarded to local air traffic control facilities, where officials decide whether to accept them.

The initiative comes as the nation's busiest airports handle millions of flights annually.

According to DOT, approximately 6.5 million flights operate each year at the nation's 30 busiest airports. About 300,000 receive reroutes before departure, while 3.6 million experience airborne reroutes, vectoring or holding.

The FAA initially limited SMART's rollout to the National Capital Region in September before beginning validation efforts with air route traffic control centers in Miami, Jacksonville and Atlanta in October.

The agency plans to continue testing the system as it works toward expanding SMART to all 22 air traffic control centers nationwide.

While the early results involve a relatively small share of domestic U.S. flights, DOT says the technology is intended to help airlines operate more predictable schedules and ease pressure on air traffic controllers.

For travelers, the Trump administration's goal is fewer delays for passengers, shorter flights and less time lost to flight congestion.

item.title: Congress returns to brutal lame-duck stretch with shutdown deadline, leadership races: 'Closet is full of s—'
item.description: Lawmakers return to Capitol Hill facing a government shutdown deadline, the farm bill and a debt ceiling fight before Democrats take power in January.
item.content:encoded:
Lawmakers are back on Capitol Hill this week for the first time since the midterm elections, and Republicans have a slew of responsibilities in front of them before Democrats take over the reins of power in January.

"The lame duck is like that closet in your house where everybody's throwing a bunch of s--- into it," Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, told Fox News Digital. "And the closet is full of s--- now, and now we got to figure out how to get it all out of there."

Current federal funding levels run out on Dec. 11, and without another deal in place, Congress risks plunging the government into another shutdown. Some Democrats signaled to POLITICO that they could use President Donald Trump’s war in Iran as leverage in spending talks — which could very well lead to a fiscal cliff that could paralyze federal agencies.

But one House Republican, granted anonymity to speak candidly, told Fox News Digital they expect another short-term extension of current funding levels, called a continuing resolution (CR), through February or March of next year. The current CR was passed to cover the end of the last fiscal year ending Sept. 30 through next month.

TRUMP SIGNS GOVERNMENT FUNDING BILL, AVOIDING A SHUTDOWN AHEAD OF MIDTERMS

"No one wants a shutdown, I would think," that House Republican said. "Not even Dems."

HOUSE GOP VOTES TO PUNT GOVERNMENT SHUTDOWN BATTLE TO AFTER NOVEMBER MIDTERMS

Other legislative priorities Congress will have to reckon with in the next few weeks include the farm bill, which is passed every five years and sets food and agriculture policy for the country. Republicans are also aiming to pass a bill to revitalize the country’s transportation infrastructure and a bipartisan tax package before the end of the year.

Then there is also the looming debt ceiling deadline coming in January, which Trump will likely call on Republicans to deal with before Congress changes hands.

GOP lawmakers shared varying levels of optimism when asked about how productive they would be.

"It can be. It should be," Rep. Marlin Stutzman, R-Ind., said. "But my faith in some of my Senate colleagues is not real high, because I feel like they have a personal vendetta towards the president, and it's more about that than it is about passing legislation. We should do our business in Congress."

Rep. Nathaniel Moran, R-Texas, said, "I think it's gonna be difficult to get a whole lot done. But we have done a lot of work leading up to the lame-duck session to prepare for passing a number of important bills, many of which are bipartisan."

But first, both House and Senate Republicans will need to face their losses in person — and consider how to rebuild.

WHAT THE 2026 MIDTERM RESULTS MEAN FOR CAPITOL HILL

"It’s going to feel like a funeral," Rep. Nicole Malliotakis, R-N.Y., told Fox News Digital. "It’s depressing even for those of us who won, because we lost so many good, quality members."

The first order of business this week will be choosing their new leaders for the next Congress.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., is running for the minority leader role unopposed for now.

And House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., is vying for the minority leader role against House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio.

MIKE JOHNSON'S NO 2 LAUNCHES GOP TAKEOVER BID AS HOUSE FALLS TO DEMOCRATS

But Moran and Stutzman both said Republicans would unify quickly after that drama is resolved.

"It should be immediate," Stutzman said. "If we're not paying attention to the American people, and we're focusing on leadership positions and personality fights, we're gonna continue to lose."

HOUSE GOP LAUNCHES DEFENSE PLAN TO SHIELD TRUMP FROM LOOMING DEMOCRAT INVESTIGATIONS

Moran said, "We understand now more than ever how important it is for us to come back together, coalesce and to regroup for the next election, and to prepare for the defense of democracy."

On Democrats’ side, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., is expected to glide into the speaker role after leading his party to a commanding victory.

Democrats’ leadership elections will take place the week after Republicans’ do.

And on the productivity front, Stutzman also called on the Senate to pass the election security-focused SAVE America Act, which Republicans are attempting to accomplish via the budget reconciliation process to sidestep the need for Democrat support. The House passed a blueprint for the bill in July.

Senate Budget Committee Chair Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has been working on the structure of that package for some time, but wasn’t so sure that if Republicans lost, it would be something the GOP had the political will to finish.

"It might turn to some people's attitudes in terms of support for it," Johnson said.

Then there’s permitting reform, which was on thin ice heading into Election Night until the White House and Senate Democrats struck a deal for a variety of wind projects to move forward. Whether Democrats support that now, and give Trump and the GOP a win on their way out, remains to be seen.

"First thing we need to do is make a motion to add a 13th month to the calendar, because we've got so much stacked up to do that's really important for the country," Sen. James Lankford, R-Okla., told Fox News Digital.

item.title: RILEY GAINES: Voters sent two midterm messages, and Democrats will only hear one
item.description: Voters in Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington backed women's sports protections even while electing Democrats in the midterm election.
item.content:encoded:
I’ll admit it. Tuesday night was disappointing.

I expected Republicans to lose more seats than they flipped. History suggested as much. But I certainly didn’t expect the results to be quite that bad.

Still, buried beneath the headlines celebrating Democratic victories was a rather inconvenient development for the political left. Americans may have voted to elect Democrats, but that doesn’t mean they’ve suddenly developed an appetite for the progressive social agenda again.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS

In fact, on one of the most contentious cultural issues of the last several years, voters delivered a remarkably consistent message.

Keep men out of women’s sports.

In Arizona, Colorado, Nebraska and Washington, voters backed measures protecting female athletic competition on the basis of biological sex.

And these weren’t just Republican strongholds. Colorado and Washington are reliably blue states whose political leadership has spent years embracing progressive gender policies.

Yet the same electorate willing to put Democrats in positions of power also voted to reject a central pillar of the modern progressive agenda.

I don’t know how much clearer voters can make themselves.

WASHINGTON STATE VOTERS APPEAR TO PASS FIRST-EVER BALLOT MEASURE SEPARATING BOYS AND GIRLS SPORTS

For years, elected Democrats and their allies in the mainstream media have insisted that protecting women’s sports is an extreme position and that anyone who dares advocate for it is a hate-filled bigot. And believe me, that’s one of the nicer things I’ve been called.

We’ve been told that acknowledging biological differences between men and women is transphobic. That girls who object to sharing locker rooms or competing against male athletes are the problem. That sports should prioritize inclusion and kindness, even when doing so comes at the expense of fairness and safety.

I’ve personally experienced what happens when you challenge that orthodoxy. I’ve also watched countless female athletes lose opportunities, endure public ridicule and face enormous pressure to remain silent simply for asking for something as basic as a fair shot.

I’ve watched politicians, university administrators and athletic organizations bend themselves into knots trying to explain why women should be expected to sacrifice their own opportunities in the name of inclusion.

WOMEN WHO FACED BIOLOGICAL MALES IN GIRLS' SPORTS AND LOCKER ROOMS SPEAK OUT AHEAD OF WASHINGTON STATE VOTE

Voters made their position clear in 2024, when the Republican agenda prevailed nationally. Apparently, even after voting for Democrats in 2026, they still aren’t buying what the progressive left is selling on this issue.

Consider Colorado.

Opponents of the girls’ sports initiative reportedly raised roughly $4 million, with substantial backing from unions and progressive organizations, including Planned Parenthood. Proponents raised approximately $200,000, largely through grassroots efforts.

They prevailed despite being outspent nearly 20 to 1.

That’s a staggering disparity, and an even more telling result. At what point does the political left accept that this is a losing issue and give it a rest?

Women’s sports protections are not some fringe position held exclusively by Republicans. The issue cuts across party lines, and the people who have spent years insisting otherwise have a serious problem on their hands.

The cultural shift is evident well beyond the ballot box.

Look at the response WNBA player Sophie Cunningham has received.

LIZ PEEK: THERE MAY BE A SILVER LINING IN TRUMP'S BRUTAL MIDTERM DEFEAT

After publicly expressing support for protecting women’s sports, Cunningham didn’t issue a groveling apology. She wasn’t shunned into professional exile. Quite the opposite.

Her public profile exploded. Her social media following and engagement skyrocketed. Her merchandise became some of the most sought-after in the league, and her Adidas shoes reportedly sold out almost immediately.

On Halloween, I saw countless young girls wearing her jersey and dressing up as Sophie Cunningham.

The notion that expressing a common-sense view about women’s sports is automatically a career-ending offense looks increasingly ridiculous.

For years, corporations, celebrities and athletes were conditioned to believe that stepping outside progressive orthodoxy would destroy their reputations.

That threat doesn’t carry quite the same weight anymore.

And I think that’s worth celebrating, particularly after an election that otherwise gave conservatives plenty of reasons to believe a serious reckoning is overdue.

But there’s another part of Tuesday’s results that Republicans would be foolish to ignore.

DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY’RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING

Affordability is a real problem. And I believe that was the bigger message voters sent on Tuesday by voting for Democrats.

Americans are tired of working harder just to afford less. They’re tired of watching their grocery bills climb, calculating how much they can spend at the gas pump and wondering whether homeownership will ever be a realistic possibility.

Young people, in particular, are confronting an economy that often feels stacked against them. And when they express their frustration, they’re too often dismissed as lazy or entitled.

Sometimes that criticism is warranted. Most of the time, it isn’t.

I believe Americans have remarkably short memories about just how bad inflation became under the Biden administration. But telling a struggling family that things used to be worse isn’t going to make their next grocery bill any easier to pay.

People vote based on the lives they’re living, not just the economic statistics politicians would prefer they remember.

And when people feel financially desperate, promises of sweeping government intervention can sound awfully attractive.

That’s part of what makes socialism so dangerous. The promise of essentially free everything is appealing, particularly to generations that have never been adequately taught its historical consequences. Of course, nothing is actually free. The bill always comes due, whether through higher taxes, mounting debt or diminished economic opportunity.

JACKSON THOMPSON: WASHINGTON STATE DEMOCRATIC PARTY CALLS GIRLS' SPORTS INITIATIVE UNCONSTITUTIONAL

But dismissing every voter concerned about affordability as ignorant or entitled would be a serious mistake.

I understand why people are frustrated. Republicans should, too.

But I don’t think the voters’ message of "affordability" in voting for Democrats is what Democrats will hear.

Elected Democrats will be tempted to interpret their victories as permission to expand DEI mandates, advance gender-transition policies for minors, allow boys access to the girls’ locker room, raise taxes, advocate for more lax immigration policies and continue placing ideological priorities ahead of the concerns of ordinary families.

Those are two very different mandates.

TREY GOWDY: THE MIDTERMS WERE A PAINFUL LESSON THAT REPUBLICANS CAN'T SKIP LEARNING

Winning an election doesn’t mean voters have endorsed every plank of your platform. And it certainly doesn’t mean they’ve abandoned their common sense.

Tuesday’s ballot initiatives should serve as a warning against making that assumption.

They should also give Republican lawmakers in politically competitive states some much-needed confidence.

Take Pennsylvania, where legislation protecting women’s sports has faced significant political resistance.

For too long, some Republicans have treated this issue as politically radioactive, apparently convinced that defending female athletes is too controversial to be worth the fight.

Well, voters in Colorado and Washington just offered a pretty compelling rebuttal.

If these protections can earn majority support in states that routinely elect Democrats, what exactly are Republicans in purple states so afraid of?

Of course, winning at the ballot box doesn’t mean the fight is over.

MATT CALKINS: AFTER YEARS OF THREATS AND INTIMIDATION, THE BULLIES IN THE WOMEN'S SPORTS DEBATE FINALLY LOST

Colorado’s newly elected Democratic governor, Phil Weiser, has already suggested that the state’s transgender-related ballot measures may need legislative adjustments.

And we’ve seen elsewhere, including Maine, how officials such as Secretary of State Shanna Bellows have resisted efforts to restrict male participation in girls’ sports.

I fully expect more legal challenges, political maneuvering and attempts to weaken these protections.

But those efforts only reinforce the larger point. When the public is given a direct say, the progressive establishment doesn’t always like the answer.

For a party that prides itself on defending democracy, it might consider respecting the democratic process even when the outcome is inconvenient.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

As for the next two years, Democrats will have an opportunity to show Americans what their governing priorities actually are.

And if recent history is any indication, I suspect they’ll provide plenty of reminders of why voters rejected their national agenda in 2024. For some reason, this is the hill they continually choose to die on.

Republicans, meanwhile, have work to do. They need to take affordability seriously, offer credible solutions and stop assuming that winning the cultural argument automatically translates into winning elections. It doesn’t.

Voters can agree with you on cultural issues and still vote against you when they feel their financial concerns aren’t being addressed. Tuesday’s midterm election results proved that these realities can coexist, and Republicans would be wise to recognize it.

Still, I refuse to confuse one disappointing election night with a wholesale cultural reversal.

I’ve spent years speaking with parents, students and female athletes across the country. I’ve seen firsthand how much the conversation has changed.

People who once whispered their concerns are increasingly willing to say them publicly. They’re less intimidated by the accusations, less willing to accept obvious contradictions and less interested in being lectured by institutions that have spent years squandering their trust.

That’s not something that disappears because one party has a good election night.

Political power changes hands. Cultural convictions are often much harder to reverse.

Democrats won important elections Tuesday. Republicans should take those losses seriously, learn from them and make the necessary adjustments.

But the voters also made something unmistakably clear once again. They haven’t suddenly decided that women and girls are undeserving of their own athletic categories, free from mediocre men.

And if the progressive left believes Tuesday was a mandate to resurrect every unpopular cultural crusade Americans have spent years rejecting, they’re in for a rude awakening.

Democrats may have won the election. They haven’t won the culture.

item.title: Gunman who killed 6 in Poland's Krakow square dies in hospital after police shootout
item.description: The Krakow shooter, 24, died Monday after police shot him during Saturday's mass shooting that killed six and wounded 15 in the historic square.
item.content:encoded:
The gunman who killed six people and wounded 15 others in a shooting at a crowded square in Poland died Monday after being shot by police during the attack, authorities said.

The 24-year-old suspect had been hospitalized in critical condition since Saturday's shooting in Krakow and underwent several operations before his death.

Polish prosecutors have opened an investigation into the killings and attempted killings, including attacks on police officers, as a possible terrorist offense.

Authorities said the gunman held far-right views, though investigators have not publicly established a motive for the attack.

TEEN WEARING HELMET CAMERA KILLS WORKER AT POLISH SCHOOL AMID FEARS OF COPYCAT ATTACKS

Police also discovered the bodies of the suspect's mother, father and sister at the family's home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, roughly 93 miles northeast of Krakow, per reporting from The Associated Press. The three are believed to have died from gunshot wounds, though authorities have not confirmed the circumstances of their deaths.

The suspect, who was wearing military-style clothing and a bulletproof vest, drove into Krakow's historic Main Square on Saturday before opening fire, according to authorities.

Four women and two men were killed, including a British man and an Austrian woman. Five foreign nationals were among the wounded. 

Two police officers injured while stopping the gunman remained hospitalized as of Sunday, though both were reportedly conscious.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

item.title: Border Dem poised to wield ICE purse strings rejects socialist ‘defund’ push
item.description: Rep. Henry Cuellar rejects the "Abolish ICE" movement, saying most Democrats oppose defunding the agency but want stronger oversight and rail guards.
item.content:encoded:
A longtime Democratic House member representing a southern border district said Immigration and Customs Enforcement is not going anywhere as "Abolish ICE" became a rallying cry for more than a dozen progressive Democrats elected or reelected in the midterms.

While the elections brought a new class of Democratic Socialists of America members to Congress, Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, told Fox News Digital that they make up just "one part of the spectrum" and that there are many "blue dogs" like himself who value strong border and immigration policies.

"I don't believe in defunding ICE and I think the majority of the Democrats do not believe defunding ICE, but there are serious rail guards we need put on ICE," Cuellar said.

Cuellar also warned Democrats against returning to the Biden administration’s border policies.

DEM REP SETH MOULTON SAYS PARTY HAS NO IMMIGRATION PLAN, IS ONLY ‘OPPOSITION TO TRUMP’

"We just can't open up the border and just say anybody that wants to claim asylum can come to the borders. That policy under Biden administration — I hope that every Democrat running for national office doesn't do that anymore," Cuellar said.

Cuellar, who is currently the ranking member of the Homeland Security Appropriations Subcommittee, is poised to become chairman, giving him significant influence over how funding for ICE is allocated.

The congressman's district includes Laredo, where Border Patrol has a major presence. Cuellar has repeatedly broken with his party on immigration enforcement, including voting with Republicans in January to approve a DHS funding bill that included billions for ICE, though he later opposed a $70 billion Republican-backed enforcement package over concerns about oversight.

Cuellar has criticized ICE for pursuing immigrants without criminal records, even though federal law allows the agency to arrest people for civil immigration violations. He has also called for greater oversight of the agency.

"Anybody that thinks that what ICE is doing, going after nuns, going after pastors, going after dreamers, they think that's normal? I don't think [so]," Cuellar said, attributing the blue wave in Texas to Trump's immigration enforcement tactics.

The Abolish ICE movement became a flashpoint for the Trump administration amid sweeping immigration enforcement operations in major cities including Minneapolis, Los Angeles, Chicago and New Orleans. The operations have resulted in more than 1.3 million arrests and 1.2 million illegal immigrants being deported or leaving the country, according to the White House.

Democrats and immigrant rights activists have criticized ICE's tactics, which include targeting courthouses, churches and job sites, as well as conditions in detention centers. The agency has also faced fierce backlash over the fatal shootings of two American citizens by ICE agents in Minnesota just weeks apart in January 2026.

In the months that followed, Democratic governors in New York, California, Connecticut, Illinois, Maryland and Minnesota signed laws restricting local and state cooperation with federal immigration officials.

DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE

Meanwhile, ICE’s partnerships with Texas authorities have expanded through 287(g) agreements that allow local officers to assist with immigration enforcement, jail screening and administrative warrants. Texas law now requires most county sheriffs to seek these agreements.

Cuellar said local law enforcement should have a limited role:

"I think the local sheriff should report somebody that’s there illegally. I think that’s it. But anything beyond that, I think we need to have a discussion," Cuellar told Fox News Digital.

Like Cuellar, Texas Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa has been highly critical of ICE's tactics. At a rally in January, she criticized Gov. Greg Abbott for directing state agencies to make Texas land and facilities available for federal immigration detention.

During her time in the state House, Hinojosa voted against a 2017 bill requiring local law enforcement to cooperate with federal agencies.

But Hinojosa has never called for Texas to follow New York and other blue states' lead in ending all cooperation with ICE.

"She is from the border from Brownsville," Cuellar said. "I haven't heard her say that she supports the defunding ICE. I don't think she has said that. Does she probably believe in transparency and rail guards for ICE? Again, I don't want to speak for her, but I think she does."

Hinojosa has also sharply criticized Abbott’s Operation Lone Star, calling the operation a political "grandstand."

Operation Lone Star launched in March 2021 amid a sharp rise in border encounters that began in 2020 and accelerated after President Joe Biden took office. The operation deployed Texas DPS officers, National Guard troops and local law enforcement to combat illegal crossings, human smuggling and drug trafficking before expanding to include state arrests and prosecutions for illegal entry, construction of border barriers and migrant transportation.

In a recent CBS interview, former Border Patrol Chief Raul Ortiz said the Biden administration sent mixed messages to migrants and accused some officials of "embracing the chaos and crisis" at the southern border.

DEMOCRAT GINA HINOJOSA STUNS ABBOTT, MAKES HISTORY AS FIRST LATINA TEXAS GOVERNOR

Cuellar agreed with Ortiz's assessment that the Biden administration didn't do its job securing the border.

"The Biden administration had it wrong," Cuellar said.

Cuellar also criticized Abbott's deployment of Operation Lone Star, pointing to a January 2024 standoff in Eagle Pass, where Texas authorities seized control of Shelby Park and restricted Border Patrol’s access.

"You still got to work with border patrol, regardless if it's a Democrat or Republican at the White House itself," Cuellar said. "So I can understand why there was that criticism, but still the Governor should have done a better job working with us at the federal level. And I hope that this new governor — and I think she will — work with us."

Cuellar said there needs to be balance and nuance in how immigration policy is carried out and that he wants to work with Trump and Republicans over the next two years.

"There are Democrats who are willing to work with the administration, with President Trump, but it takes two to have a deal," Cuellar said.

DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement to Fox News Digital that deportations will continue.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"Our mission is simple and non-negotiable: secure the border, protect American lives, and control everything and everyone coming into this country. We are focused on getting the job done and enthusiastically partner with any official dedicated to achieving that goal," CBP Assistant Commissioner Hilton Beckham said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

Fox News Digital reached out to Hinojosa for comment.

item.title: The stoning of Stephen Miller, now running the Trump White House
item.description: Trump's decision to name Stephen Miller his new chief of staff sparked an unprecedented media firestorm, as critics quickly targeted his hardline immigration record and influence over the president's agenda.
item.content:encoded:
When Donald Trump made the stunning announcement that Stephen Miller is his new chief of staff–preempting the New York Times by a few minutes–I literally said:

"Watch for a barrage of negative Miller stories in the next couple of days."

I was wrong.

It was the next couple of hours.

‘LAWYER UP’: DEMS IMMEDIATELY PUT TRUMP ON NOTICE AMID REPUBLICANS' MIDTERM BLOODBATH

MS NOW anchor Katy Tur said: "Donald Trump’s whole immigration agenda is Stephen Miller, and for Stephen Miller, it has always been absolutist: do whatever is necessary, as much as we can possibly do, be as cruel as possible as a warning sign for anybody who might want to come over." 

WHITE HOUSE SHAKEUP CONTINUES WITH NEW DEPARTURE FROM TRUMP ADMINISTRATION

"Stephen Miller, one of his most notorious staffers, will instead be taking over as chief of staff," CNN anchor Kaitlan Collins said from the White House driveway, adding: "He was one of two staffers, including Kristi Noem, who came out after Alex Pretti was killed in Minneapolis and called him a domestic terrorist." 

That New York Times story: "Miller, a deeply ideological Trump loyalist, has been the architect of some of the most polarizing domestic policies in Mr. Trump’s second term." 

The conservative Federalist cited a past Miller comment on mass deportations: "At every turn illegal aliens have always been treated better than Americans."

And then there are the Democrats. Rep. Robert Garcia, the expected incoming House Oversight chairman, said: "Stephen Miller is the architect of the unconstitutional ICE raids that have terrorized our communities and kidnapped and killed American citizens and immigrant families… Stephen Miller should lawyer up."

Oh, and incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries called him "a dangerous xenophobe."

Of course, it’s a huge story, and should be covered as such. It’s about his record, and, putting aside the adjectives, it’s fair game. My purpose here is not to either defend or criticize Miller, who has been one of Trump’s most powerful aides since the first term.

Miller is, without question, one of the hardest of hardliners.

I cannot remember this kind of all-out artillery attack, seconds after a top White House appointment was announced. I don’t think anything else comes close.

And the sheer velocity and global reach of this negativity is being fueled in the digital battleground of social media.

That evening was just the first line of shock troops, who struck as soon as Trump announced that Miller would replace Susie Wiles, who has battled breast cancer, as his top aide. By the next morning, the cavalry had arrived.  

The Wall Street Journal called Miller an "advocate of the no-holds-barred style of governing that delighted the president’s most die-hard MAGA supporters—and was repudiated by much of the rest of the country on Election Day."

Axios, describing Miller’s view of nearly unlimited presidential powers, said of Trump: "He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints." 

The New York Post, headlining the old beer ad "It’s Miller Time," said that choosing the "pugnacious" official "removes almost all hope that the nation’s partisan warfare will ease after the elections." The president is "going to bring his pit bull along."

TRUMP NAMES STEPHEN MILLER NEW WHITE HOUSE CHIEF OF STAFF, REPLACING SUSIE WILES

The Times, in its pair of stories, played some of the 41-year-old Miller’s greatest hits.

"Those include separation of migrant families at the border; the 2017 Muslim travel ban, directing the government to stifle critics of Mr. Trump; the ending of nearly all U.S. refugee programs; the widespread pressure campaign against American universities; extrajudicial boat strikes that have killed hundreds; and purges of officials deemed insufficiently loyal to Mr. Trump."

Miller also unleashed the military, "pitting masked, heavily armed immigration agents against residents of cities like Minneapolis and Chicago." Fact-check: True.

Maureen Dowd, not to be outdone, denounced the "gaudy, corrupt, vice-ridden, heartless rule, we have been living in Trumpsville. The demonic Trump conjured an American hell."

Miller hasn’t exactly stayed silent. He said Trump is "the most transformative political leader" in our history and has "single-handedly saved America from those who would destroy it." 

A day after the election, Miller led a call about pushing forward with mass deportations and, the Times reports, did not even mention the Democratic avalanche that was partially a protest against such policies.

The president says he loves watching the combative Miller on TV–a key credential for any Trump staffer.

Miller is certain to back Trump’s assaults on the mainstream media, ranging from denunciations and lawsuits to whether the press corps should be evicted from the White House. 

Shortly before the election, Miller said on Elon Musk’s X that the Democrats have nominated candidates "who are all extremist, freaks and America-hating lunatics." Miller urged voters to "send a message to the corrupt media, corrupt Democrats and corrupt left-wing politicians who want to steal your future."

It’s not hard to see why Miller has a target on his back.

But imagine that Miller, who also urged his boss to wind down the Iran war, never joined the administration. Wouldn’t Trump still have pursued all these tough policies, starting with mass deportation? Clearly, it’s the commander-in-chief who decides.

TRUMP ‘HOLDS ALL THE CARDS’ IN WAR AGAINST IRAN’S REGIME, WHITE HOUSE SAYS

Other top aides and Cabinet secretaries have certainly been raked over the coals.

The media weren’t kind to Karl Rove, dubbed "Bush’s brain," the strategist who was investigated in a CIA leak case but never charged.

Some were accused of being too close to the industries they regulated. Ronald Reagan’s Interior secretary James Watt ripped the environmental movement as a clash between "liberals and Americans," and the Sierra Club collected more than 1 million signatures seeking his ouster.  

But none of them were pummeled with the fierce intensity that has enveloped Miller.

As for the coming investigations, Todd Blanche announced that "the chief of staff already has a lawyer. The attorney general of the United States and the Justice Department." With those words, the AG confirmed again that his department serves as the personal law firm of Trump and his acolytes.

Look, Stephen Miller is a brawler, the opposition party is spoiling for a fight, and that should provide the press and public with plenty of pounding in the political ring. But while Miller is now the most important staffer of Donald Trump’s last two years in office, remember, he is still a staffer.
